blocks.text: **The problem.** An undirected graph has `n` vertices, `0` to `n - 1`, and `graph[u]` lists the neighbours of `u`. The graph may be in several pieces. Return `true` if the vertices can be split into **two teams** so that every edge joins a vertex of one team to a vertex of the other — that's a **bipartite** graph.

blocks.alt: Left: four vertices in a square, coloured blue and orange alternately, so every edge joins the two colours: bipartite. Right: a triangle. Vertices 0 and 1 get different colours, but 2 is next to both, so whichever colour it takes, one edge (shown in red) joins two vertices of the same colour: not bipartite.

blocks.code:
graph = [[1,3],[0,2],[1,3],[0,2]]         ->  true    (teams {0,2} and {1,3})
graph = [[1,2,3],[0,2],[0,1,3],[0,2]]     ->  false   (0, 1, 2 form a triangle)
graph = [[1],[0],[]]                      ->  true    (vertex 2 can join either team)

blocks.text: The idea: the colours are forced

Give each team a colour. Pick any vertex and colour it **0**. Now there's no choice left: each of its neighbours must be **1**, each of *their* neighbours must be **0**, and so on through the whole piece. So just walk the graph — BFS works well — giving every new vertex the opposite colour of the vertex that found it.

If the walk ever finds an edge whose two ends already have the **same** colour, the graph can't be bipartite: every colour on the way was forced, so no other choice could have avoided the clash. That clash always comes from a cycle of **odd** length — a graph is bipartite exactly when it has no odd cycle.
A new piece of the graph is the one place you do get a choice: nothing connects it to what's already coloured, so start it with colour 0 too.
There are 2ⁿ ways to put n vertices into two teams. Try each one — bit `i` of a number is the colour of vertex `i` — and check every edge.
**Time O(2ⁿ · (V + E)), space O(1).** Every colouring is checked against every edge. Fine for 10 vertices, hopeless for 100 — and it ignores the fact that one vertex's colour decides all the others.

Keep a `color` array, `-1` for *not coloured yet*. For every uncoloured vertex, start a BFS that colours it 0; each vertex taken from the queue gives its uncoloured neighbours the other colour, and checks that its coloured neighbours really do have the other colour.

blocks.caption: Every colour after the first is forced. Try the odd cycle to see the clash.

blocks.text: **Time O(V + E), space O(V).** Each vertex is coloured and queued once, and each edge is checked from both ends. A DFS that passes the colour down works just as well; BFS simply avoids deep recursion.

blocks.alt: Every colouring: O(2ⁿ·(V+E)) time, O(1) space. BFS colouring: O(V+E) time, O(V) space.

blocks.text: The jump from exponential to linear comes from one observation: after the first vertex of each piece, no colour is ever a choice.

items: **Several pieces** — each needs its own start, which is why the outer loop tries every vertex.
**An isolated vertex** — `graph[u]` is empty; it fits in either team.
**A tree, or any even cycle** — `true`: trees have no cycles at all, so nothing can clash.
**Possible Bipartition** — people who dislike each other must go to different groups: build a graph from the dislike pairs and run the same check.
**Detect a cycle** — the other half of this pattern: remember the parent instead of a colour. Previous lesson.
**Three or more colours** — with k ≥ 3 colours the choices are no longer forced, and no fast method is known; only small inputs can be solved, by backtracking.
